name: Phase One: Assess Readiness
title: Phase One: Assess Readiness
answer: Phase One: Assess Readiness is the first step in piloting AI in a school or district, where leaders check whether people, policies and support systems are actually ready before tools are rolled out. It matters because readiness is about training each group for their own work and finding barriers early, not about counting devices. Skipping this step lets predictable problems, especially equity gaps, surprise a district later.

sections.body: Readiness in this idea is not a question of how many devices a district owns. It means giving each group of people practical training that connects AI to their own daily work, so a counselor understands how an early warning flag is built and a second grade teacher understands what a reading tool does with a child's voice. It also means identifying barriers before they cause trouble, since obstacles tend to arrive in linked clusters such as missing guidance, limited training and disagreement about what AI education means. Because fixing one barrier often eases several others, the readiness check turns each gap into a concrete action item with a date. Equity sits inside this check from the beginning rather than being added later.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice the readiness check can be a short worksheet asking whether the district has an approved tool list, a data privacy process, a named owner for AI decisions, training for staff, and a plan for students without devices or internet at home. Each gap found becomes an action item with a date. The text does not give separate grade band steps, but it does describe how readiness looks for different roles, with a counselor needing to know how an early warning flag is built and a second grade teacher needing to know what a reading tool does with a child's voice. Every pilot should carry an equity plan from the start, so if a tool is meant for homework the pilot finds out how many students lack a device or reliable internet and what those students will do instead. Districts often lend hotspots or keep library and computer lab time open after school for this reason, and the plan should also cover students with disabilities and English learners, whose results are looked at separately when the pilot ends.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this idea with research support and cites several studies. Luckin et al. (2022) describe readiness as practical training that helps each group understand AI in their own work rather than a general course on how AI works. Wang and Cheng (2021), a study of two schools in Hong Kong, found obstacles in linked clusters such as missing guidance, limited training and disagreement about what AI education means, and also found schools waiting for government guidance while government waited for school examples. Wang et al. (2026), a study of nearly 4,500 sixth graders in the Netherlands, found that family income affected achievement directly and that classroom AI use did not change that advantage, while digital literacy mattered more.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits on what readiness can promise. Handing out AI tools without teaching students to use them wisely should not be expected to close gaps on their own, since the Dutch study found classroom AI use did not change the income advantage. Equity planning must be built into every pilot rather than treated as an afterthought, and it must account for students without devices or reliable internet at home, students with disabilities and English learners, whose results are reviewed separately. The readiness worksheet exists so that gaps become dated action items instead of surprises, which keeps decisions with named people rather than with the tools. The text does not describe legal duties, so this is a description of practice rather than legal advice.
